findings.title: Second downsize definition silently overrides the existing width/height API
findings.body: Lines 145-151 define OptimizedImage.downsize twice: first as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) and then as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}). In Ruby the second definition replaces the first, so any existing caller using the four-argument width/height form will now either raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or have its max_width value interpreted as a complete dimensions string. This is an API/contract break for other thumbnail/downsize callers, not just the new uploads-controller caller.

findings.title: Percentage downsizing is incompatible with the animated-GIF instructions
findings.body: The new upload path passes dimensions "80%" with allow_animation taken from SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When that setting is true and the file is a GIF, optimize() dispatches to downsize_instructions_animated, which forwards "80%" to resize_instructions_animated as the argument to gifsicle's --resize-fit. --resize-fit expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage scale (gifsicle uses a different option for scaling), so animated GIF downsizing will fail; convert_with returns false, the controller ignores that result, retries the same failing command up to five times, and then proceeds with the still-oversized file.

findings.title: Downsize result is ignored and the loop neither guarantees nor verifies the size limit
findings.body: The while loop at lines 66-69 calls OptimizedImage.downsize up to five times but discards its boolean return value and performs no check after the loop. If conversion fails, produces a larger file (possible when re-encoding formats such as PNG without a quality/compression change in downsize_instructions), or five 80% reductions are still not enough to get under SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb, create_upload silently continues to Upload.create_for with an oversized/corrupt intermediate file. The feature therefore either fails later with the old size error after expensive retries or stores an upload that does not satisfy the stated invariant.

findings.title: In-place conversion uses the same path for input and output
findings.body: OptimizedImage.downsize is called with tempfile.path as both source and destination. The downsize instructions run ImageMagick `convert <file>[0] ... <file>` (and for animated images gifsicle with --output set to the input file), rather than converting to a separate temporary file and atomically replacing the original only on success. Tools that truncate/create the output before fully consuming the input, or that fail part-way, can leave the user's only uploaded copy truncated or corrupted; because the return value is ignored and ensure only closes the tempfile, the corrupted file is then passed to Upload.create_for instead of preserving the original upload.

findings.title: Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores configured image and attachment limits
findings.body: validateUploadedFile previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], which distinguishes images from attachments and respects admin configuration; it now always allows 10 * 1024 KB. If an admin configures a lower limit, the client will accept and upload files the server then rejects (the server-side downsizing only applies to images, so oversized attachments are uploaded in full just to fail), and if an admin configures a higher limit, the client incorrectly blocks valid uploads. The hardcoded value also makes the file_too_large message report 10240 KB regardless of the actual configured limit.

findings.title: 413 error handler reports a fabricated 10 MB maximum
findings.body: In displayErrorForUpload's 413 branch, the message previously used Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb and now always interpolates 10 * 1024 KB as max_size_kb. A 413 is generated by the web server/proxy limit, which is unrelated to this constant, so users will be told the limit is 10 MB even when the proxy or site setting allows far less or more, sending them to retry with files that will continue to fail.
